observations.prose: The corpus addresses readers directly with 'you'/'your' throughout, treating them as already caught inside the systems under analysis—workers facing algorithmic pricing, users blocked by dickovers, citizens watching gerontocracy. The address creates solidarity rather than instruction; the reader is implicated in the argument, not merely its recipient.

'We' appears throughout as a broad collective—workers, citizens, internet users—that includes writer and reader against a named opponent class. It does not mark an institution or an editorial stance. Place it when naming shared exposure to a system; shift to 'you' when the action required falls on the reader alone.

First-person singular grounds abstract argument in lived experience—cancer treatment and literary executor arrangements anchor a piece on political gerontocracy; a childhood as a bookseller motivates a meditation on AI economics. The anecdote arrives briefly, performs a structural job (analogy or credentialing), and yields back to argument; the writer appears as arguer and exemplar, not as biographical subject.

Contractions are the unmarked, default register; the prose reads as spoken argument throughout, in analytic and polemical passages alike. A full form gains rhetorical weight precisely because it is rare—reserve it for deliberate emphasis rather than standard negation.

Uncontracted negatives are sparse against the contracted default, landing with deliberate extra weight. Where a contraction would slide past, 'cannot' or 'do not' stops the reader and signals a claim the writer is unwilling to soften. The assembler pairs this absence with the contractions measurement.

Profanity appears across all samples as a punctual intensifier at moments of moral indignation—'tax the shit out of empty homes,' 'the whole fucking point'—not as ambient texture. Place it to mark the logical apex of an outrage; one well-placed instance per piece is the pattern, not scattered deployment.

Questions serve three roles: structural pivots that title or open a section, Socratic challenges placed inside an opponent's position, and reader-directed moves softened from imperative to question. Direct imperatives also appear—'Stop using Chrome, switch to Firefox'—aimed at readers who must take a concrete step. Both forms appear in every sample.

Parentheses carry running asides, self-corrections, and sardonic glosses—'(a direct quote)' appended to a paraphrase, '(very, very weird)' amplifying an adjective. They interrupt the main clause briefly; content is typically one phrase or short sentence, functioning as a low-key register brake present across every sample.

En-dashes perform the pivoting and appending work that em-dashes conventionally handle—abrupt additions, mid-sentence redirects, appositive amplifications. They appear across every sample and are the sole dash-based interruption mark in the corpus. Use them consistently; do not substitute an em-dash.

Em-dashes are entirely absent across the corpus. The interruption and aside roles are filled by en-dashes and round parenthetical spans. The assembler pairs this absence with the en-dashes and round-parenthetical-spans measurements.

The prevailing mode is confident assertion. When hedges appear—'I think,' 'of course'—they typically introduce a concession the argument immediately overturns. Predictions are stated as near-certainties; genuine uncertainty markers are reserved for attributing positions to opponents, not for softening the writer's own claims. Place hedges to signal fair-mindedness before a rebuttal.

Named opponents—Thiel, Musk, Trump, Uber, Facebook—are quoted directly and then systematically dismantled; their own words supply the rebuttal target. Allied sources are credited by name and extended rather than merely summarized. Third-party coinages are acknowledged by attribution: 'John Gruber's term,' 'what Douglas Rushkoff calls.'

Analogies draw from economics, legal procedure, and history and are extended to their logical limit before the punch-line names the contradiction: the US as an escrow agent who keeps both deed and money; Trump's diplomacy as a poker game with the table flipped; gig 'flexibility' as risk-transfer. A figure typically runs two to four sentences.

Pieces open with a hook—a quoted aphorism, a compressed thesis ('Data brokers are a cancer'), or a framed paradox ('Here's an irony')—that the body systematically unpacks. Closings return to the opening's frame or escalate to a broader systemic claim; the final sentence typically reframes the specific topic as symptom of a structural problem, often in a short declarative.

structured_output.gaps: All ten samples fall within a fifteen-day window in July 2026; the register is consistent but the corpus cannot confirm whether these habits hold across longer periods or in shorter link-post formats. Personal biographical detail appears but functions structurally—anecdote serving argument—and should not be treated as factual content for reuse in drafts. No editorial mediation is disclosed; punctuation choices, dash selection, and register can be attributed to the writer directly.
